summary: Defines a wildcard Pseudowire Type for LDP-based pseudowire signaling. Normally both ends must use the same type in each direction. With the wildcard, only one endpoint needs to be configured with the type, and the other learns it, simplifying setup. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people building a bridge need to agree on the kind of bridge. This lets one person decide, and the other just says okay, whatever you choose.

questions: what is the wildcard pseudowire type
how to configure pseudowire type on one endpoint
subtitle: A codepoint that lets one pseudowire endpoint decide the protocol type for both directions.

tldr.problem: Pseudowire signaling normally requires both endpoints to be pre-configured with the same Protocol Type, but sometimes the configuration is most easily done at just one endpoint.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a special wildcard Pseudowire Type value (0x7FFF) that signals the other endpoint to determine and return the type, without requiring prior knowledge.
tldr.outcome: Simplifies pseudowire setup in gateway scenarios where the type is known at one endpoint but not at the other, particularly useful for layer 2 network gateways.

today: RFC 4863 is a Standards Track document and defines a widely-implemented mechanism for simplifying pseudowire configuration. It remains the specification for wildcard pseudowire type support in LDP-based systems.

sections.title: The Problem: Coordinating Pseudowire Types
sections.content:
In pseudowire technology, two Provider Edge routers (the endpoints) must agree on what type of traffic they are carrying across an MPLS network. Both endpoints traditionally need to be preconfigured with the identical Pseudowire Type (PW Type) value.

This works fine in most cases, but creates challenges in certain setups. For example, a PE router serving as a gateway between a layer 2 network and remote attachment circuits might receive setup requests from the layer 2 side that lack information about which PW Type should be used. The PE knows the type (because its local circuit determines it), but the far-end PE does not and cannot know it without being told.

The traditional approach requires the unconfigured endpoint to wait for a Label Mapping message to learn the type before starting its own signaling. This adds complexity and delay.
sections.plainLanguage: When building a bridge between two towns, you need both towns to use the same kind of bridge. Normally both towns have to decide and agree ahead of time. But what if one town already knows what kind they want?

sections.title: LDP-Based Pseudowire Signaling
sections.content:
This RFC builds on Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) based pseudowire signaling, defined in RFC 4447. In LDP signaling, each pseudowire endpoint initiates the creation of a unidirectional LSP (Label Switched Path) independently. Both endpoints send Label Mapping messages that must carry the same PW Type for the pseudowire to function correctly.

The RFC assumes the reader is familiar with the Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) architecture, which defines how protocols other than IP are carried across MPLS networks. It references RFC 3985 for architectural details and RFC 2119 for the standard keywords MUST, SHOULD, and MAY that define requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP is like a messaging system between routers. Each router sends a message saying what type of traffic it wants to carry. The type has to match on both sides.

sections.title: The Wildcard Type Solution
sections.content:
RFC 4863 introduces a new Pseudowire Type codepoint: 0x7FFF, called the wildcard type. When a PE sends a Label Mapping message with this value, it signals the receiving PE to perform two tasks: first, determine the actual PW Type for both directions of the pseudowire, and second, signal that type back in its own Label Mapping message.

The wildcard type has special matching semantics: it matches any valid PW Type other than itself. This allows the far-end PE to respond with whatever type it is configured to use.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of deciding the bridge type before you start, you can say 'you decide' (the wildcard), and the other side tells you what they want.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving the Wildcard FEC
sections.content:
When a PE wishes to initiate pseudowire signaling without knowing the PW Type, it sets the type to wildcard (0x7FFF). The targeted PE receives this and, following normal procedures for checking the Attachment Group Identifier (AGI) and Target Attachment Individual Identifier (TAII) values, responds by treating the message as if the wildcard had indicated its own configured PW Type.

If the targeted PE is not configured with a specific non-wildcard PW Type, it must reject the request with a Label Release message and a 'Generic Misconfiguration Error' status code.

If a PE that sends the wildcard receives a Label Mapping message with a PW Type it cannot support, or if the response is itself wildcard, it must likewise reject with an error message. Once the PE receives a supported PW Type from the far end, it uses that value for both directions of the pseudowire.
sections.plainLanguage: The requesting router says 'you pick'. The other router picks its type and sends it back. If either side says 'I cannot do that', they send an error message and the setup fails.

sections.title: Security and Operational Constraints
sections.content:
The wildcard mechanism itself does not change the fundamental security of LDP pseudowire signaling. Message exchanges remain the same as in RFC 4447. However, an attacker attempting to connect to an access circuit requires one less piece of configuration information.

To mitigate this risk, the RFC recommends that a PE receiving a wildcard FEC should only proceed with setup if explicitly configured to accept wildcards for the particular Attachment Individual (AI) in question. Further, operators should apply the full security considerations of RFC 4447, particularly those pertaining to the Generalized PWid FEC Element.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting one side pick is simpler, but routers should only allow it for circuits they trust, so attackers cannot misuse the feature.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content:
RFC 4863 requests one IANA allocation from the Pseudowire Type registry defined in RFC 4446 (IANA Allocations for PWE3): the codepoint 0x7FFF for the wildcard type.

This single registry entry enables the entire mechanism described in the RFC. No other protocol allocations are required.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority set aside one special number (0x7FFF) in the Pseudowire Type list to mean 'you decide'.
